lessons.title: What SQL Is and How Finance Uses It
SELECT, FROM and WHERE on Finance Data

slots.practicalActivity: In your course SQL environment, run the SELECT/FROM/WHERE query from Lesson 2 against ap_invoices_all filtering for invoice_amount >= 5000, giving the table an alias written the Oracle way (no AS). Then extend it with ORDER BY to sort by invoice_amount descending and add FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY to cap the result, confirming your output changes correctly when you flip the sort to ascending.
slots.deliverable: A working, run SQL query against ap_invoices_all combining WHERE, a bare table alias, ORDER BY and FETCH FIRST, with both ascending and descending output captured.

lessons.title: Working with Dates in Oracle SQL

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run a query against ap_invoices_all that filters invoice_date using a sargable date range for a specific month (rather than wrapping the column in TRUNC), then separately write a query that checks a nullable column (such as a discount or hold-reason column) with IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, confirming NVL produces a safe default instead of a NULL in your result set.
slots.deliverable: Two run queries: a sargable date-range filter on invoice_date, and an IS NULL/NVL-guarded query against a nullable column, both against ap_invoices_all.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for SQL Foundations for Finance: take the three finance questions you wrote down in Lesson 1's lab and, for each one, write the actual SELECT/FROM/WHERE query that answers it using only what this chapter covered (filtering, sorting, dates, NULLs) -- no joins yet. Run all three and sanity-check that each result set looks like a real, plausible answer to the question you originally wrote.
slots.deliverable: Three run SQL queries answering the three finance questions from Lesson 1's lab, using only single-table SELECT/WHERE/ORDER BY/date/NULL techniques.

lessons.title: Inner vs. Outer Joins for Finance

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run the INNER JOIN between poz_suppliers and ap_invoices_all from Lesson 6, filtered to invoices over $10,000 and sorted by amount descending. Then write and run the LEFT OUTER JOIN plus IS NULL pattern from Lesson 8 twice: once to find suppliers with zero invoices, and once to find invoices with no payment yet, confirming both result sets look plausible against your practice data.
slots.deliverable: Three run queries: a filtered supplier/invoice INNER JOIN, a zero-invoice-suppliers LEFT OUTER JOIN, and a no-payment-yet LEFT OUTER JOIN.

lessons.title: Joining Journals to Ledgers and Periods

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run a join chain on the Receivables side linking customer transactions to receipts and applications, mirroring the Payables pattern from the previous slot. Then write and run a join from GL_JE_HEADERS to GL_PERIODS on PERIOD_NAME, filtered to a single real or invented period, confirming every journal line in that result actually falls inside that period's date range.
slots.deliverable: A run Receivables transaction/receipt/application join, plus a run journal-to-period join filtered to one period.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Joining Financial Tables: write and run your own fourth join-based investigation not given verbatim in any lesson -- for example, suppliers whose invoices are all fully paid versus suppliers with at least one unpaid invoice -- using the INNER JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN patterns from this chapter. Document the exact business question your query answers before showing the SQL.
slots.deliverable: One original join-based investigation query (business question plus the SQL answering it), run against the practice schema.

lessons.title: Totals with SUM, COUNT and GROUP BY

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run the per-supplier outstanding-balance query from Lesson 11's lab (SUM, COUNT, GROUP BY on payment_status_flag <> 'Y'), then add a HAVING clause filtering to only suppliers with an outstanding total over $10,000. Finally, write and run the full five-bucket aging CASE/GROUP BY query from Lesson 13 against ap_payment_schedules_all, sorted by total_outstanding descending.
slots.deliverable: A run per-supplier outstanding-balance query with a HAVING filter, plus a run five-bucket aging report sorted by total outstanding.

lessons.title: Balances by Supplier, Customer and Period

slots.practicalActivity: Extend the aging query to break totals out by both supplier and bucket at once (two-column GROUP BY), confirming each supplier can appear in more than one bucket row. Then write and run a window-function query (SUM ... OVER, ordered by period) producing a running total of invoice amounts per supplier over time, and compare it against a plain GROUP BY total to confirm the running total only ever increases.
slots.deliverable: A two-dimension (supplier-and-bucket) aging breakdown, plus a running-total window-function query compared against its GROUP BY equivalent.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Aggregation and Aging: build one combined report query that totals outstanding Payables by both aging bucket and business unit (if your practice data has more than one BU) or by aging bucket and supplier otherwise, using GROUP BY, HAVING to exclude any bucket under $1,000, and ORDER BY to rank the largest exposures first. Write a one-paragraph summary of what the result tells a treasury team about upcoming cash needs.
slots.deliverable: One combined aging-by-bucket-and-dimension report query with a HAVING floor and a written treasury-facing summary of the results.

lessons.title: Finding Missing Records with NOT EXISTS

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run the correlated subquery from Lesson 16's lab, finding invoices priced above the average for their own supplier. Then rewrite the same logic as a CTE (WITH clause) to avoid repeating the subquery, and finally write and run the NOT EXISTS version of the 'invoices with no payment yet' question from Lesson 18, confirming it returns the same rows as the LEFT OUTER JOIN version from Chapter 2.
slots.deliverable: A correlated-subquery and an equivalent CTE version of the above-supplier-average query, plus a NOT EXISTS query confirmed to match an earlier LEFT OUTER JOIN result.

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run a duplicate-detection query that finds invoices sharing the same supplier, invoice number and amount (a likely duplicate-entry pattern) using GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Then write and run a set-comparison query (using NOT EXISTS, INTERSECT, or MINUS depending on what your Oracle version supports) comparing this period's set of paid invoices against last period's, identifying invoices that appear in one period's paid list but not the other.
slots.deliverable: A duplicate-invoice-detection query using GROUP BY/HAVING, plus a two-period paid-invoice set-comparison query.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Subqueries and CTEs: write your own business question -- "which suppliers have an invoice this quarter with no matching payment at all" -- and solve it two different ways, once with NOT EXISTS and once with a CTE plus a LEFT OUTER JOIN, confirming both return the same result set.
slots.deliverable: One business question solved two independent ways (NOT EXISTS and CTE/LEFT OUTER JOIN), with both result sets confirmed identical.

lessons.title: Answering Business Questions: The Unpaid Invoices Challenge

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run the full invoice-vs-paid reconciliation query from Lesson 21 (LEFT OUTER JOIN, NVL, GROUP BY, HAVING difference <> 0), then do the same for the Receivables mirror image (cash receipts vs. applications). Finally, build the complete unpaid-invoices-over-$10,000-and-more-than-30-days-old query from Lesson 23 -- the course's running challenge -- joining suppliers, invoices and payment schedules, and run it against your own practice data.
slots.deliverable: A run Payables reconciliation query, a run Receivables reconciliation query, and the completed unpaid-invoices-over-$10,000 challenge query run against real practice data.

lessons.title: Tracing a Payment Back to the Invoice
Reconciling AP and AR to General Ledger with SQL

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one payment from your practice data and write a query tracing it backward through AP_INVOICE_PAYMENTS_ALL to the specific invoice(s) it settled, confirming the traced amount matches what you'd expect. Then write and run a reconciliation query comparing Payables (or Receivables) subledger totals to the GL_JE_LINES balance for the same period, using JE_SOURCE to isolate only subledger-generated journals, and record whether the two totals tie.
slots.deliverable: A payment-to-invoice trace query, plus an AP/AR-to-GL reconciliation query with a documented tie (or gap) result.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Investigating Financial Data: run the full unpaid-invoices challenge query from Lesson 23 a second time with tightened thresholds (over $5,000, more than 60 days old) and verify the result set shrinks sensibly. Then write a one-page investigation report, as if for a controller, walking through your reconciliation and tracing results from this chapter and naming any exceptions you found.
slots.deliverable: A re-parameterized unpaid-invoices query with verified results, plus a one-page controller-facing investigation report covering this chapter's reconciliations.

lessons.title: SQL Practice Set: Ledger and Close Investigations

slots.practicalActivity: Work through and run all three Payables investigations from Lesson 26 (top-5 exposed suppliers, possible duplicate payments, suppliers missing a remit-to site) against your own practice data, then build and run the lab's own fourth investigation (suppliers with a recent invoice and no payment applied). Then build the Receivables and Ledger/close mirror-image investigations for Lessons 27 and 28, using the same join/aggregate/subquery toolkit.
slots.deliverable: Four run Payables investigation queries plus matching Receivables and Ledger/close investigation queries built with this course's full toolkit.

slots.practicalActivity: Run EXPLAIN PLAN FOR and DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY against your slowest-looking query from this course, and rewrite any WHERE clause that wraps a date column in TRUNC into a sargable range instead, confirming the plan changes. Then take one query you've written in this course and turn it into a reusable report: parameterize its hard-coded thresholds (the $10,000, the 30 days) as bind variables or a view, so it can be rerun with different inputs without editing the SQL text itself.
slots.deliverable: An EXPLAIN PLAN before/after comparison for one rewritten sargable query, plus one of your own queries turned into a reusable, parameterized report.

slots.practicalActivity: Course-closing capstone: in one sitting, rebuild the complete unpaid-invoices-over-$10,000-and-more-than-30-days-old query from memory, without looking at Lesson 23, then run it and confirm it matches your earlier result. Follow it with the duplicate-payment check and the AP-to-GL reconciliation query, also from memory, and write a two-paragraph reflection on which of this course's techniques (joins, aggregation, subqueries/CTEs, or reconciliation patterns) you'd reach for first on a brand-new, never-seen finance question.
slots.deliverable: Three from-memory, independently rebuilt and run queries (unpaid invoices, duplicate payments, AP-to-GL reconciliation) plus a written reflection on technique priority for new finance questions.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can write real, production-quality Oracle SQL against Oracle Financials tables -- filtering, joining, aggregating, using subqueries/CTEs, and reconciling AP, AR and GL data -- to answer real finance investigations such as the unpaid-invoices-over-$10,000 challenge, and can read an execution plan and turn a working query into a reusable, parameterized report.
